title: Series and Parallel Circuits
learning_goal: Analyze, design, and construct series and parallel circuits and explain how current and voltage behave in each arrangement.

stages.title: 1. A complete circuit
stages.content: Electric current flows only when there is a closed conducting path and a source of potential difference. Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to represent batteries, resistors, switches, and other components.

stages.title: 2. Series circuits
stages.content: In a series circuit, components share one path. The same current passes through each component, and the source voltage is divided among the components.

stages.title: 3. Parallel circuits
stages.content: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points. Each branch has the same voltage, while current splits among the branches.

stages.title: 4. Worked comparison
stages.content: If one bulb is removed from a simple series circuit, the only path is broken and all bulbs go out. In a parallel circuit, other branches can still conduct current when one branch is opened.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: Three bulbs are connected in parallel to the same battery. One bulb burns out. What happens to the other two bulbs?
stages.hint: Each parallel branch has its own path to the battery.
stages.alternate_explanation: Removing one branch does not break the complete paths through the other branches.
stages.answer: The other two bulbs remain on.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, read circuit diagrams, distinguish series from parallel connections, predict what happens when a component is removed, and explain current and voltage behavior in each type.

concept_cards.title: A complete circuit
concept_cards.content: Start at the battery's positive terminal (the long plate). Trace a conducting path through the bulbs and back to the negative terminal. Series means one loop through both bulbs. Parallel means separate branches between the same two junctions.

concept_cards.title: Series circuits
concept_cards.content: In a series circuit, components share one path. The same current passes through each component, and the source voltage is divided among the components.

concept_cards.title: Parallel circuits
concept_cards.content: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points. Each branch has the same voltage, while current splits among the branches.

concept_cards.title: Two resistors are in series in one unbranched loop. Compare their currents.
concept_cards.content: In steady state charge does not accumulate between components. The same current passes through each series component.

concept_cards.title: Two resistors are connected in parallel across an ideal battery. Compare their voltages.
concept_cards.content: Both branches connect the same two circuit nodes. Equal voltage does not imply equal currents when resistances differ.

concept_cards.title: What happens when a path is opened?
concept_cards.content: An open switch creates a gap. In series the gap breaks the only loop, so both bulbs go out. In parallel the other branch keeps its complete path and stays on. With an ideal battery, the voltage and current in the intact branch stay the same; the battery supplies less total current.

worked_examples.prompt: In the diagram, 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors form one series loop across an ideal 9 V battery. Why do they carry the same current?
choices: The larger resistance uses up more current
hint_steps: Identify the physical quantities, interactions, or model named in the question.
Explain the cause before choosing the conclusion.
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: In steady state charge does not accumulate between components. The same current passes through each series component.
alternate_explanation_steps: In steady state charge does not accumulate between components. The same current passes through each series component.
Check the assumptions stated in the prompt. Apply the relationship to this situation rather than choosing by a familiar keyword.

solution_steps.equation: One loop → the same current at every point
solution_steps.explanation: There is no junction where charge can split into another path, and charge does not build up between the resistors in steady state.
Add resistances because both resistors lie along the only path.
The battery, the 3 Ω resistor, and the 6 Ω resistor each carry 1 A.

solution_steps.equation: V₁ = 1 A × 3 Ω = 3 V; V₂ = 1 A × 6 Ω = 6 V
solution_steps.explanation: The voltage drops add to 9 V. The current is the same, but the voltage divides according to resistance.

worked_examples.prompt: Reconnect the same 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors in parallel across an ideal 9 V battery. Find each branch voltage and current, then the total battery current.
worked_examples.answer: 9 V across each branch; 3 A through 3 Ω; 1.5 A through 6 Ω; total 4.5 A
accepted_answers: 9 V across each branch; 3 A through 3 Ω; 1.5 A through 6 Ω; total 4.5 A
hint_steps: Identify the physical quantities, interactions, or model named in the question.
Explain the cause before choosing the conclusion.
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: Both branches connect the same two circuit nodes. Equal voltage does not imply equal currents when resistances differ.
alternate_explanation_steps: Both branches connect the same two circuit nodes. Equal voltage does not imply equal currents when resistances differ.
Check the assumptions stated in the prompt. Apply the relationship to this situation rather than choosing by a familiar keyword.

solution_steps.explanation: Trace both branch ends: each branch starts at junction A and ends at junction B. Both therefore span the entire battery voltage.
Use the full 9 V across the upper 3 Ω branch.
The lower branch has twice the resistance, so at the same voltage it carries half the current.

solution_steps.equation: I_total = I₁ + I₂ = 3 A + 1.5 A = 4.5 A
solution_steps.explanation: The current splits at A and recombines at B. Charge is conserved; neither branch uses up current.
Adding a second path lowers the equivalent resistance below either branch resistance. This is smaller than the 9 Ω series total.
